signals.title: Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU
signals.excerpt:
Meituan releases the weights for LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model built for AI agents. It was trained entirely on Chinese hardware and performs at the level US models like Claude Opus 5 reached a few months ago on coding benchmarks.

The LongCat team at Chinese food delivery company Meituan has released the weights for LongCat-2.5, one week after the model's official unveiling. LongCat-2.5 is built for agents that work through long, multi-step tasks autonomously, particularly coding. According to Meituan, it comes close to top Western models on several benchmarks.

LongCat-2.5 is a mixture-of-experts model that activates only a subset of its specialized subnetworks for each token it processes. Out of 1.6 trillion total parameters, roughly 48 billion are active per token. Through the API, the model handles up to one million tokens at once and generates responses up to 128,000 tokens long. It understands text, images, and video, responds in text, and lets users toggle reasoning on and off.

...

Meituan quantizes the experts' weights and activations to 4-bit precision, which Chinese chips can process natively. In Meituan's load tests, throughput rises 43.3 percent for prompt processing and 42.77 percent for response generation compared with an 8-bit version. Meituan says accuracy stays on par with the uncompressed model.

This version is available in a separate repository. The self-hosting guide describes a cluster of 194 Huawei Ascend accelerators from the Atlas A2 series. Two handle image processing, 64 handle prompt ingestion, and 128 handle response generation. There's no guidance for Nvidia GPUs.

...

The LongCat team reports 88.4 points on Terminal Bench v2.1, a benchmark that measures how well agents solve command-line tasks. Meituan lists Claude Opus 5 at 89.1, GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, and Deepseek-V4.1-Flash at the top of the table with 90.6.

DeepSWE tests how well models fix bugs in real code repositories. Here LongCat-2.5 jumps from 9.7 to 64.6 points, placing it behind every other model in the table except Claude Opus 4.8, with Deepseek-V4.1-Flash leading at 74.2 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 72.7. The more recent Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol are not included in the table.

...

Terminal Bench v4.0, the harder variant, puts LongCat-2.5 at 38.5 points, slightly above GPT-5.6 Sol's 37.3 but well below Opus 5's 53.9. The model posts 91.9 on the web search benchmark BrowseComp, the highest score in the table, though Meituan ran this test in its own environment.

# llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem 

Published November 13, 2026 

 ggml-org

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

...

Today we release libraries `v1.0.0`, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

### Releases 

| Release | Library | Public header(s) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| llama.cpp v1.0.0 - LLM inference in C/C++ | `libllama` | `llama.cpp/include/` |
| ggml v1.0.0 - Tensor library for machine learning | `libggml` | `ggml/include/` |

...

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

...

### Backend and model coverage 

The underlying machine learning engine of `llama.cpp` - `ggml` is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

signals.title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
# When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with

...

AI-Generated Summary 

- GLM-5.3 NVFP4, a quantized mixture-of-experts model with 753 billion parameters and 40 billion activated per token, requires about 464 GB of GPU memory, exceeding the 252 GB HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU.
- Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve the model through one OpenAI-compatible endpoint using tensor parallelism (TP=2), with each GPU holding and computing roughly half the weights.
- vLLM launches a distributed service across both Stations, enabling multi-token prediction, FP8 KV-cache storage, and prefix caching to maximize throughput under concurrent load.
- AIPerf benchmarks on the SPEED-Bench Coding dataset show overall output throughput peaking at 607.8 tokens per second at concurrency 16, then falling to 385.0 tokens per second at concurrency 32 with mean request latency of 453.5 seconds.

...

Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs. 

The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.

Before starting, connect the two Stations with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook.

This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.

...

This step turns two machines into one service: the same launch script runs on both Stations, reads `~/glm53.env`, and starts one vLLM rank on each. Two settings matter most if you adapt it: `--max-model-len 98304`, the context ceiling in tokens, which covers input plus output, and `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.93`, which gives vLLM 93% of GPU memory. If you change other flags, change one at a time and test again.

...

At this point one model spans two machines. Neither GPU holds a complete copy, and neither can answer a request alone: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.

...

`RDMA_CHECK_OK` means the check passed with no warnings. In `nvidia-smi`, A shows the `VLLM::Worker_TP0` process and B shows `VLLM::Worker_TP1`, one rank per GPU. The startup log reports about 218 GiB of weights per GPU, roughly half the checkpoint, which confirms that the model is split across the two GPUs.

...

Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.

| Configured concurrency | Overall throughput (tok/s) | Mean request latency (s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean inter-token latency (ms/token) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 107.4 | 49.84 | 479.75 | 8.78 |
| 8 | 386.0 | 114.17 | 433.79 | 19.01 |
| 16 | 607.8 | 136.46 | 482.90 | 23.77 |
| 32 | 385.0 | 453.54 | 899.36 | 77.90 |

 Table 2. SPEED-Bench Coding results with prefix caching enabled, four MTP draft tokens per step, and an FP8 KV cache. Latency metrics are means over measured requests; warmup is excluded. TTFT measures time to the first token, which may be reasoning

Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.

...

You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory. That opens up work that’s hard to do on a hosted endpoint: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs.

signals.title: Neo4j releases Relate, an open source in-memory database built for AI agents
signals.excerpt:
## The short version

- Relate is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and built in Rust
- It runs in-process, in memory, with optional disk storage for durability
- It includes an MCP server, a command-line tool, and Bolt and HTTP query endpoints
- Errors carry retryable flags, and a row cap stops large results from flooding an agent
- Neo4j cites Gartner: machine users reach 75% of database workloads by 2029

...

Neo4j, a company that makes graph databases, has released Relate. A graph database stores information as things and the connections between them, which suits questions like "who is linked to whom, and through what." As Cyprus Shipping News reported, Relate is open source, written in the Rust programming language, and aimed at AI agents and the systems built around them.

...

Connectivity comes built in. Relate has a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a common standard for letting agents use outside tools, plus a command-line tool. It also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints, so existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks and developer tools should work with it.

## Graph queries and retrieval

Relate supports Cypher, the query language Neo4j uses for graph data. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity, which finds items with similar meaning, and follow connections through the graph in the same step. Neo4j says this supports multi-hop reasoning, where an answer depends on following several links in a row, and GraphRAG, which feeds a model facts drawn from a graph. The company says this gives agents more accurate results and fewer hallucinations, meaning invented answers. That claim is Neo4j's and is not tested in the source.

The release says Relate is 100% openCypher compliant and more than 97% compliant with GQL, the standard graph query language. Those numbers suggest queries written for other graph systems may carry over, though the source does not say how that was measured. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license, a permissive open source license.

signals.title: Build a production-grade RAG Agent: Part 2 - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Yuvraj

 Posted on Nov 16 • Edited on Nov 16 

# Build a production-grade RAG Agent: Part 2 

Let's build the agent and its tools, in TypeScript with the Vercel AI SDK. The ideas carry over to any language or framework, such as Python with Pydantic AI.

The repo has two folders that run on their own and meet only over HTTP: `harness/`, the measure from Part 1, and `agent/`, which you build here. Its README covers the rest.

This is Part 2 of a two-part series:

- Part 1 - The evals. Measuring and deciding what "good" means.
- Part 2 - The agent: tools, the loop, one change at a time

TL;DR

In Part 2, we build the agent: one model, three tools over a library of tax Acts, and a loop. By the end, we have an agent that beats the first iteration (0.582 → 0.729, with confidently wrong answers down from 5 to 0), and a way to spot a real improvement.

...

The repo ships the three Acts as files in `agent/data/law/`, and a ready-made SQLite library built from them. Copy it in before you start the agent: 

```
npm run seed                 # copies the ready-made library: 5,694 passages and their vectors
npm run seed -- --fresh      # downloads the Acts again and embeds every passage: about a minute and $0.20

...

Next, tools. They let the agent search and read the law, the "retrieval" in RAG, so it answers from sources instead of memory.

> Design tools like APIs: one job each, with a clear set of arguments. Keep the number of tools low and each one simple.
> 
> Tool result = data for model; Tool failure = response for the model to act on

A tool essentially looks like this:

...

execute: (input) => call(() => searchPassages(library, book, input)),
}),

...

The description is the tool's manual: the model reads it every time.

The repo has these tools:

- `library_search`: finds an Act by its title or by what it covers. Nothing it returns can be cited.
- `passage_search`: searches inside the Acts by a query, exact words or a section code, and returns the first 300 characters of each hit. Nothing here can be cited either.
- `library_read`: reads a whole section, or an Act's outline. Only what it returns can be cited, as `[extract:L1]`.
- Optional, with `TOOLS=library,web`: `web_search` and `web_read`, for law and official guidance the library lacks. Web search needs a Firecrawl key.

The first three are the default, and all the agent needs.

## Step 4. The Research Agent 

Now the agent itself. It reasons about the question, calls tools, reads what they return, and answers once it has enough. This is a ReAct agent, named after the 2022 paper ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.

We build this by using the SDK's `generateText`: 

```
// agent/src/agent.ts, trimmed: the floor's call, with tools and a way to stop
const result = await generateText({
  model,
  instructions: instructionsFor(names, today),
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: questionMessage(question, country) }],
  tools,                                                   // library_search, passage_search, library_read
  stopWhen: [isStepCount(limits.rounds + 1), overBudget],  // 40 rounds of tools, or $3
  prepareStep,                                             // after the last round: tools off, so it must answer
});

```

That's the whole loop. The SDK calls the model, runs the tools it asks for, sends back the results, and repeats until the model answers without asking for a tool, or a limit stops it.

signals.title: An Agent That Searches, Outlines, and Reads Entire Documents Outperforms Chunk-and-Embed Retrieval
signals.excerpt:
# Retrieval for RAG-Resistant Docs An agent that searches, outlines, and reads entire documents outperforms chunk-and-embed retrieval

Published Nov 13, 2026

Retrieving documents chunk by chunk works well with many types of text, but it can fail with documents in which the meaning of a given span — say, numbers in a table — depends on particulars found elsewhere on the page — say, the label of their units. Researchers assigned agents to keep all the necessary information in view. 

What’s new: Sagar Tamang, Ayush Vyas, and Tabarakul Hazarika at Indian Institute of Technology Patna and TwoSpoon, an independent tech lab, developed Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search (READ). Their method replaces vector-based retrieval with an agentic harness and specialized search tools. 

Key insight: For RAG-style retrieval, a document is divided into chunks that are embedded, and a model retrieves chunks whose embeddings are similar to the embedding of the query. But this approach can fail with documents such as financial or scientific reports, where numbers in a table gain important meaning from units or dates that may lie many lines away, or legal briefs, in which words may have special meanings that are defined many paragraphs away. An agent with tools to navigate undivided documents can look beyond predefined chunks.

How it works: The authors used the READ method with Gemini 2.5 Pro.

- The system had access to three tools: (i) A keyword-search tool returned matching line numbers, (ii) an outline tool listed section headings with line numbers, and (iii) a text-reader tool fetched specific line ranges.
- Given a query like, “What is the mathematical difference between the Fiscal Deficit and the Revenue Surplus for the year 2024-2025?,” the READ agent activated a loop that generated a search term such as “Fiscal Deficit,” scanned a document for the term, checked matching line(s) against the document outline, and read the text from the table headers to the matching line(s).
- Within the loop, the model refined its query when it got too many hits, too few hits, or insufficient information to make sense of what it found. Each refinement repeated the loop with a new search term or a new range to be read.

Results: The authors used READ, RAG-style retrieval, and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop to answer 51 questions about a 780-page financial report published by the government of Gujarat, India. All systems were based on Gemini 2.5 Pro. READ answered 58.8 percent of the questions correctly, outperforming both RAG-style retrieval (15.7 percent) and RAG-style retrieval in an agentic loop (27.5 percent)

signals.excerpt:
# Huawei open-sources MACaQ quantization tool for model compression

The story

Huawei has released MACaQ, an open-source tool that squeezes large language models down to a fraction of their size without the usual multi-machine setup. The company says it can compress a 122-billion-parameter model to 4-bit precision in about 64 minutes on a single GPU, a job that normally demands far more hardware and time.

Quantization, the process of storing a model's weights at lower precision, is how big models get small enough to run on modest machines. Doing it fast, on one GPU, lowers the barrier for researchers and smaller companies that cannot afford sprawling clusters, and it fits Huawei's broader push to build an AI stack that does not depend on restricted Western chips.

signals.title: Edge0 Releases 145B and 120B Sparse MoE Models for Single-GPU SSD Streaming
signals.excerpt:
# Edge0 Releases 145B and 120B Sparse MoE Models for Single-GPU SSD Streaming

Edge0 released Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, open-weight sparse MoE models that run on single 24GB GPUs via SSD streaming and native 4-bit NVFP4 quantization.

...

On November 13, 2026, open-source AI developer Edge0 released Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, two open-weight sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models engineered to run frontier-level agentic and coding workflows on a single 24GB consumer workstation GPU. By dynamically streaming expert weights from NVMe solid-state storage, the release enables academic laboratories and universities to run hundred-billion-parameter systems locally without incurring recurring cloud API expenses or exposing confidential institutional data off-premises.

...

The Edge0 project announced the public release of its two flagship open-weight models, Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, hosted on the Edge0 Hugging Face repository in native 4-bit NVFP4 and Q3_K formats alongside source code on the Edge0 GitHub repository. Derived from the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next architecture, both models are specialized for autonomous software engineering, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. Unlike conventional dense architectures requiring every parameter to reside in video memory, Edge0 implements a latent sparse MoE structure where only a tiny fraction of parameters activates per token.

The accompanying Edge0 inference runtime (edge0-infer and edge0-strata) establishes a tiered memory architecture. The GPU VRAM stores core attention layers and hot experts, while dormant experts reside in host system RAM and PCIe NVMe storage. Using predictive expert prefetching and zero-copy direct memory access (DMA), the runtime streams weights into VRAM on demand, enabling a 145-billion-parameter foundation model to run on a single desktop GPU like the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090.

...

Deploying a 145-billion-parameter large language model in traditional 16-bit precision requires roughly 290 gigabytes of VRAM—demanding an eight-GPU data center node. Even post-training 4-bit quantization requires 75 to 80 gigabytes of resident memory, far exceeding standard desktop configurations.

Edge0 addresses this constraint through native 4-bit NVFP4 training rather than post-training quantization, preserving mathematical and syntactic precision. Edge0-145B contains 48 transformer layers with 512 sparse experts per layer. The gating router activates 10 routed experts and 1 shared expert per token, yielding approximately 10.12 billion active parameters. Both models support a 256K-token context window using an int8 key-value cache, with 32K tokens retained directly in VRAM. Architectural details published on Edge0’s official documentation portal are detailed below:

...

Hardware throughput figures published by Edge0 and confirmed in technical reviews by eesel AI show that the streaming engine achieves interactive token speeds on consumer hardware. Running on a single RTX 5090 D with 24GB VRAM and a PCIe Gen 4 NVMe drive, Edge0-145B achieved peak agent decode speeds of 98.3 tokens per second, sustaining 80 to 90 tokens per second across multi-turn programming sessions. Prefill throughput reached 3,165 tokens per second at 16K context lengths.

The 120B variant demonstrated even greater throughput: prefill speeds reached 2,668 tokens per second at 4K and 4,357 tokens per second at 16K under NVFP4, while chat decoding averaged 124.9 to 130.2 tokens per second. Agent decode loops reached 135.5 to 144.6 tokens per second. On evaluation benchmarks, Edge0-145B recorded 86.5 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (measuring autonomous CLI tool execution) and 64.6 percent on DeepSWE 1.1 (resolving real GitHub repository pull requests). These figures place the open-weight release alongside proprietary commercial systems while running fully within local workstation limits as open-source software.

...

Edge0 announced that it is preparing pull requests to merge its streaming kernels directly into upstream community engines, including llama.cpp, vLLM, and Ollama, during late November and December 2026. Merging the strata streaming logic into mainstream frameworks will allow researchers to run Edge0 models through standard CLI flags without custom compilation.

signals.title: GLM-5.3 Hits 607.8 Tok/s on Two DGX Stations with vLLM
signals.excerpt:
Officially launched on November 13, 2026.

#### 💡 TL;DR

- NVIDIA benchmarked Zhipu's 753-billion-parameter GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model distributed across two DGX Station GB300 systems linked by ConnectX-8 RDMA.
- The vLLM tensor-parallel deployment achieved 607.8 tokens per second at concurrency 16 with 482ms time-to-first-token before degrading at higher loads.
- The 464GB checkpoint used FP8 KV-cache, prefix caching, and four-token speculative decoding across 252GB HBM3e GPUs in each station.

NVIDIA has published a developer blog detailing how Zhipu AI's 753-billion-parameter GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model can be served from two linked DGX Station GB300 systems, achieving 607.8 tokens per second at peak throughput. Posted November 13, 2026, by NVIDIA engineer Fatima Fall, the benchmark demonstrates frontier-scale model deployment across multiple machines behind a single API endpoint using vLLM tensor parallelism and ConnectX-8 RDMA interconnect.

...

The 464GB GLM-5.3 checkpoint exceeds the memory capacity of any single GPU, requiring a distributed approach. Fall's configuration splits the model weights across two DGX Station GB300 units, each equipped with 252GB of HBM3e memory. The vLLM framework handles tensor parallelism (TP=2), allocating approximately 218 GiB of weights to each GPU while leaving headroom for activation memory and the KV-cache.

ConnectX-8 RDMA networking links the two stations, enabling low-latency cross-machine tensor communication. The setup uses FP8 precision for the key-value cache, prefix caching to reuse repeated prompt tokens, and four-token speculative decoding to accelerate generation. Maximum model length is capped at 98,304 tokens, balancing context window size with memory constraints.

...

Peak throughput of 607.8 tokens per second occurred at concurrency 16, with a time-to-first-token of 482.90 milliseconds and mean request latency of 136.46 seconds. However, the throughput curve is nonlinear. At concurrency 32, output dropped to 385.0 tok/s while mean latency ballooned to 453.5 seconds, indicating the system hits bottlenecks beyond the optimal load point.

...

The NVIDIA developer blog was officially published on November 13, 2026. The benchmark recipe and configuration details are publicly available, though the blog does not provide vLLM configuration files or installation scripts. GLM-5.3 itself is an open-source model from Zhipu AI, accessible for local deployment by organizations with sufficient hardware.

signals.title: I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker, corrections as regression tests - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
# I made my AI agent's notes vault retrievable: 35 MB embedder, llama.cpp reranker,

...

Ok, I made a thing! LLMs have their... quirks. Namely re-reading the same notes, wandering back and forth, and spending 10x more tokens than needed because I can't be explicit.

So I built Haystack — a semantic router for a markdown vault. Instead of the agent digging through files, it queries: hybrid retrieval (embeddings + corpus-IDF term stats, RRF-fused, cross-encoder reranking via llama.cpp), all local, zero cloud, one 35 MB model, ~10 ms per query. MIT, one-command setup: github.com/diogocccarvalho/haystack.

...

Your corrections become regression tests. Every retrieval miss you fix becomes a permanent rule AND a QA pair. The audit reindexes and runs every pair — it exits 1 on a regression, so the same question can't silently fail twice.

And the learned rules only pin when they actually beat retrieval: a stored phrasing must outrank the corpus' own best hit for the same query. Scale-free, not absolute-threshold — so swapping embedders doesn't break your corrections. I A/B'd models against frozen QA sets and rejected two (a reranker that was 2x faster but -16pp Recall@3; a 97M embedder at -7pp). Numbers in docs/RESEARCH.md.

...

| English vault (68 pairs, nickname-style) | 1.000 | 0.917 |
| Portuguese vault (14 pairs, synthetic) | 1.000 | 1.000 |

...

## Try it 

```
./setup.sh --start          # model + config + embeddings server, one command
python3 haystack.py reindex
python3 haystack.py query "that thing about the invoices"

```

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works instead (Ollama, LM Studio, remote API). Python 3.11+, stdlib + numpy only — no framework, no vector DB daemon, no cloud.

signals.excerpt:
Daisytuner announced on November 16, 2026 that it had raised €6 million in seed funding and released Daisyflow, an AI inference engine that serves models inside customers’ own infrastructure and adapts their execution to different hardware.

Daisytuner reports that its first results show Qwen 2.5 running up to 18% faster than vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs. The result gives the launch a specific performance data point as the company presents Daisyflow for a broader range of model categories and accelerator suppliers.

...

At the center of the technology is docc, Daisytuner’s open-source compiler. It translates PyTorch, NumPy and C/C++ into a dataflow intermediate representation, a format that makes data movement, parallelism and computation explicit, then generates native code for NVIDIA’s CUDA and AMD’s ROCm platforms and for novel architectures. This addresses the manual performance work that can arise when a new model or chip disrupts existing optimizations.

AI agents search for optimizations and benchmark them on real hardware. docc verifies each optimization for correctness before use, and proven recipes enter a performance database. During later compilation, the compiler can match those recipes to similar code, allowing knowledge from earlier workloads to inform new optimization work.

The hosted Daisytuner Platform turns this into a developer workflow with continuous benchmarking on GitHub pushes, a browser-based optimization editor and the performance database. Users can inspect hotspots measured on real hardware, create optimization recipes and submit the results as pull requests. Daisyflow builds on that optimization layer by adding production model serving.

...

Daisyflow serves language, vision, speech and recommendation models. Its inference layer routes requests to models, batches and schedules work for hardware utilization, and coordinates multi-step and agent workflows. Applications connect through standard APIs, with OpenAI compatibility for language models, and a ready-to-use chat interface is included.

signals.title: Agentic GraphRAG Explained With 6 Enterprise Patterns
signals.excerpt:
# A Practitioner's Guide to 6 Agentic GraphRAG Patterns

How autonomous agents turn static knowledge graphs into living Context Graphs that remember decisions, user intent, and operational history

Partha Sarkar

November 15, 2026 22 min read

...

Today, enterprise implementations of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) largely fall into two foundational architectures, or deploy a hybrid of both:

1. First-Generation RAG (Vector Search): Chunking unstructured documents into high-dimensional vector embeddings and performing cosine similarity searches. Useful for simple document lookup, however, struggles with multi-hop reasoning due to lack of enterprise knowledge and frequently hallucinates when facts span different sections of a document.
2. Second-Generation RAG (Standard GraphRAG): Mapping enterprise entities into Knowledge Graphs and executing static Cypher queries or global community summaries. This grounds language models in structured ground truth, but is static, rigid, and passive. Here, an engineer crafts a prompt, a single-shot Cypher query executes against the KG, pulling subgraphs or related chunks and the retrieved context is provided to the model's context window.

...

To overcome this challenge, enterprise architectures are transitioning to Agentic GraphRAG.

...

In Agentic GraphRAG, the Knowledge Graph is no longer a passive database queried at the end of a prompt. It becomes a dynamic institutional knowledge map and an evolving Context Graph:

- The agent autonomously navigates the graph step-by-step, evaluating relationship types and dynamically deciding where to branch or backtrack.
- The graph stores not just static enterprise data, but the firm's institutional and temporal memory, such as previous business decisions, user preferences, past incident resolutions, and exceptions.
- The agent acts as a data steward, proactively monitoring operational telemetry, calculating topological blast radiuses during disruptions, and safely extracting and adding new knowledge from incoming documents.

...

## Core Components of the Agentic Graph Fabric

Transforming a passive Knowledge Graph into an autonomous, reasoning-ready Agentic Graph Fabric requires decoupling graph operations into six functional patterns:

1. The Operational Memory Graph: A graph data model that captures institutional precedents, approved policy waivers, committee rulings, and historical business exceptions as first-class connected nodes.
2. Agentic Execution Memory Engine: A graph data model that captures multi-turn tool invocations, execution parameters, error codes, and verified trajectories, enabling agents to bypass known failure paths and execute optimal tool sequences.
3. The User Context Graph Engine: An evolving personal subgraph modeling an individual user's organizational roles, ongoing project mandates, and past conversational choices, delivering seamless cross-session continuity.
4. The Self-Enriching Topology & Blast Radius Engine: A living operational graph that links baseline application topologies with continuously harvested ITSM incident histories, matching telemetry symptoms to historical root causes, IT teams activated for resolution, and affected user groups.
5. Hierarchical Multi-Scale Engine: A multi-resolution graph structure organizing dense enterprise topologies into recursive community clusters (L0 to L3), enabling autonomous agents to navigate vertically between high-level executive summaries and granular atomic facts.
6. Adaptive ReAct Graph Navigator: An incremental horizontal graph navigation loop that breaks multi-hop problem-solving into verified steps (Reason → Act → Observe), following lateral entity relationships and backtracking when encountering dead ends.

signals.title: Huawei MACaQ Promises Faster Open-Source AI Quantization
signals.excerpt:
Huawei open-sourced MACaQ, claiming 4-bit quantization of a 122-billion-parameter model in 64 minutes on about 32.5GB of GPU memory.

Nov 14, 2026· 6 min read

Huawei open-sourced MACaQ in November 2026, a quantization toolkit whose authors claim they reduced a 122-billion-parameter model to 4-bit precision in sixty-four minutes using roughly 32.5 gigabytes of GPU memory, targeting inference stacks such as vLLM and llama.cpp. Quantization—storing weights at lower bit widths—is foundational science for democratizing large models: it trades a controlled accuracy loss for memory and latency wins that determine whether a model runs on a workstation, a phone, or only a hyperscaler pod. Against a backdrop of Gemini 4 Hydrogen raising API prices and Edge0 advertising 145-billion-parameter local runs, MACaQ is a research signal that hardware efficiency races continue alongside frontier scaling.

...

Parameter counts climb faster than DRAM bandwidth. Physics limits how quickly HBM can feed matrix multiplies; reducing bits per weight directly cuts memory traffic. Post-training quantization (PTQ) without full retraining is especially valuable for open models organizations cannot afford to fine-tune at scale. A credible hour-long PTQ pass for 122B parameters would shrink operational barriers for universities and national labs lacking billion-dollar clusters.

Skepticism is warranted: vendor claims require reproduction. Huawei publishing code enables independent verification—the scientific norm. JSIPE readers should watch for third-party benchmarks on perplexity, MMLU-style tasks, and domain-specific evals after MACaQ quantizes popular open checkpoints.

...

Existing ecosystems include GGUF quant pipelines, AutoGPTQ, AWQ, and vendor-specific kernels on CUDA and ROCm. MACaQ's differentiation, per release materials, is speed at large parameter counts with modest GPU footprints—possibly via algorithmic approximations, better calibration sampling, or fused kernels tuned for Ascend and NVIDIA paths. Compatibility claims with vLLM and llama.cpp matter because those runtimes power most self-hosted deployments outside clouds.

signals.title: Alibaba Releases Qwen4-Max: 2.4T MoE, 71B Active, 1M Context - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen4-Max, the first model of its Qwen4 generation. Qwen4-Max is a proprietary sparse MoE model with a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B parameters active per token. It accepts text, images and video, and supports a 1M-token context window. Alibaba also cut API prices and reports a 62% drop in average cost per task.

...

- Size: 2.4T backbone parameters, 71B active per token, plus 328B N-gram Embedding parameters. 1M context, 393K max output tokens.
- Runs on: Hosted only: QwenCloud API, Token Plan, Qwen Studio, QwenWork and Qoder. No open weights, so no self-hosting or quantized builds.
- Performance: A large jump over Qwen3.8-Max. Competitive with frontier models on agentic work, behind on hard coding and vision.
- Best: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agent work): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1, the next-best model.

...

Qwen4 upgrades the sparse MoE design in 3 places: attention, residual connections and embeddings.

- GDN + Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA): Each QSA layer pairs with 3 Gated DeltaNet layers. These compress history into fixed-size states. QSA then uses a lightweight indexer to pick relevant context at micro-block granularity. This lowers attention and indexing cost on long sequences.
- Gated Residual (GR): 4 parallel residual branches use dynamic read and write gates. The aim is stronger information flow and better training stability.
- N-gram Embedding: 328B extra parameters provide lookups of local token patterns at layer 2. This adds capacity with little extra compute.

...

Alibaba’s comparison chart covers 16 benchmarks. Rivals are Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1. Several scores are cited from third-party leaderboards. None were independently reproduced at launch.

Qwen4-Max ranks first on 4 of 16 benchmarks:

- HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agents): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1 and 9.2 for Opus 5.5.
- Agents’ Last Exam v1.1: 46.7, versus 43.4 for Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1.
- BioMysteryBench: 85.0, versus 84.4 for GPT-6.1 Sol.
- DeepSWE v1.1: 75.7, versus 75.5 for Kimi K3.1.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads 7 of the 16 charts. Qwen4-Max trails most clearly on coding and vision:

- ProgramBench: 31.5 versus 65.0 for Opus 5.5.
- Terminal-Bench 4.0: 48.5 versus 67.2 for Kimi K3.1.
- Chartography: 54.2 versus 71.1 for GPT-6 Astra.
- Humanity’s Last Exam: 51.7 versus 59.8 for Opus 5.5.

On Alibaba’s own Work360 benchmark, Qwen4-Max scores 52.69, up from 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Work360 spans 26 top-level domains and 721 specialized fields.

...

## How can developers use Qwen4-Max?

The model ID is `qwen4-max` on QwenCloud. The API works with OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible clients. Supported features include function calling, structured outputs, context caching, batch processing, web search and fine-tuning. The default rate limit is 5,000,000 tokens per minute. Thinking mode is toggled with `enable_thinking`.

Subscription access runs through the Token Plan.

signals.title: NVIDIA releases Dynamo recipes for Korean open models — Data Phoenix
signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA releases Dynamo deployment recipes for four Korean open models 

 NVIDIA released Dynamo recipes for A.X K2, K-EXAONE 2.0, Solar Open 2 and Motif-3, outlining multi-GPU configurations for B200 systems. 

 DP News Team Nov 14, 2026 · 2 min read

...

NVIDIA released Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for A.X K2 from SK Telecom, K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research, Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies. The configurations provide model-specific starting points for serving the four open models across multiple NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

The recipes are optimized for B200 GPUs and can deliver “up to 2x performance out of the box,” according to NVIDIA, which also said they reduce deployment work. The performance figure is a company claim, not an independently verified benchmark result. NVIDIA’s release does not disclose a workload, baseline, per-model result or test environment.

Dynamo is NVIDIA’s open-source distributed inference-serving framework. In an aggregated setup, one worker pool handles both prompt processing and token generation. A disaggregated setup divides those jobs between separate prefill and decode pools; the frontend sends a request to a prefill worker first and then to a decode worker.

Dynamo’s KV-aware router weighs the relevant key-value cache state held by each worker against its decode load, then chooses the lowest-cost worker. A KV cache stores attention state from tokens the model has already processed, so reusing it can avoid repeating part of the computation. Workers can report cache changes to the router over ZMQ or NATS Core. Without those events, the router can estimate cache state from its own routing decisions.

...

The live recipe index lists aggregated and disaggregated B200 deployments for each model. A.X K2 uses eight GPUs in aggregated mode or 12 in a two-prefill, one-decode topology. K-EXAONE 2.0 uses four or eight GPUs, respectively; its disaggregated recipe uses NIXL over UCX on InfiniBand RDMA. Solar Open 2 uses four GPUs in aggregated mode or eight with one prefill and two decode workers. Motif-3 uses two GPUs in aggregated mode or eight in a three-prefill, one-decode layout.

The repository currently lists Motif-3 in its experimental section, which it describes as functional but under active development and not yet fully validated for production use.
